recycled-cotton.origin: Recycled cotton is cellulose fiber recovered from cotton textile waste. Pre-consumer (post-industrial) inputs include spinning and weaving waste, cutting-room scraps and finishing waste such as brush fiber from sueding; post-consumer inputs are used garments and home textiles. Research literature commonly cites estimates that about 75 percent of textile waste is landfilled and that less than 1 percent is recycled back into new garments, so fiber-to-fiber cotton recycling remains small relative to virgin cotton. Much recent industrial research on recycled cotton yarns comes from spinning mills and universities in Bangladesh.
recycled-cotton.structure: Chemically, recycled cotton is still cellulose, a linear polymer of beta-1,4-linked glucose, but mechanical recycling changes its physical profile. Shredding tears fabric apart, breaking fibers, lowering mean length and raising short-fiber content, neps and leftover yarn fragments; a shredder described in one study reduced fabric to individual fibers no longer than about 35 mm. Dyed inputs keep their color, and residual finishes, elastane or polyester may be present from mixed fabrics. Dust and trash particles can carry into yarn and later appear on the fabric surface.
recycled-cotton.process: Inputs are sorted by fiber content and color, trims such as buttons, zippers and labels are removed, and fabric is cut and shredded through rotating toothed cylinders into loose fiber. Arafat and Uddin (2022) note that because this fiber is short, it has traditionally been blended and rotor (open-end) spun into coarse yarns of about 10 to 20 Ne for denim, towels and home furnishings. In an industrial trial they showed that up to about 25 percent recycled cotton could be blended with virgin cotton in soft-twist 30 Ne ring-spun yarn suitable for knit tops. Chemical routes instead dissolve cotton-rich waste to make pulp for regenerated cellulosic fibers.
recycled-cotton.performance: Performance depends on the input and blend. Shorter fibers mean more hairiness, lower yarn strength and more unevenness: a 2026 study of rotor yarns with brush-fiber waste found higher mass variation, more imperfections and hairiness and slightly lower tensile properties than 100 percent virgin cotton. Rotor yarns need high twist, which makes them stiffer and less absorbent and gives a harsher hand from surface wrapper fibers. Otherwise recycled cotton behaves like cotton: hydrophilic, stronger wet than dry, flammable, and dyeable with reactive, direct and vat dyes. Pre-colored inputs can avoid dyeing and give melange effects.
recycled-cotton.identify: Recycled cotton cannot be distinguished from virgin cotton by burn testing (indicative only; both burn quickly with a paper-like smell and soft grey ash) or by FTIR, since both are cellulose. Length testing reveals a larger short-fiber share and microscopy may show more broken ends and fragments, but neither proves recycled origin. Recycled-content claims therefore rest on chain-of-custody documentation rather than fiber testing, while contamination by polyester or elastane from mixed inputs can be detected by solubility tests or FTIR.
recycled-cotton.labeling: The generic fiber name remains cotton under the US Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. In the US, a recycled claim is also an environmental marketing claim, and the FTC's Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260) require recycled-content claims to be substantiated. Textile Exchange's Recycled Claim Standard and Global Recycled Standard are voluntary chain-of-custody certifications that verify recycled input, with the Global Recycled Standard adding social, environmental and chemical requirements. Fibers regenerated from dissolved cotton waste are labeled as regenerated cellulosic fibers, not as cotton.
recycled-cotton.past: Reclaiming fiber from textile waste has a long history, including the nineteenth-century trade in shoddy made from wool rags and the use of cotton and linen rags for papermaking before wood pulp. Cotton spinning waste has long gone into coarse yarns, wiping cloths and batting. Current work aims to raise recycled shares in finer yarns: studies since 2022 have tested ring spinning with pre- and post-consumer recycled cotton, direct use of pre-colored brush-fiber waste in rotor yarns, and the contamination that cotton waste yarns leave on woven fabric surfaces.
facts: rotor spinning into about 10 to 20 Ne coarse yarns
up to about 25% recycled cotton in 30 Ne yarn (2022 study)
Textile waste recycled into new garments

recycled-nylon.origin: Recycled nylon is polyamide made from waste rather than from virgin monomer. The two main textile polymers are nylon 6, polymerized from a single monomer, epsilon-caprolactam, and nylon 6,6, made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid. Inputs include pre-consumer waste such as polymer purge, off-specification chips and yarn and fabric waste from spinning and weaving, and post-consumer items such as discarded fishing nets and carpets. Fishing nets are predominantly nylon 6 and a major source of marine plastic pollution, which has made them a prominent feedstock for chemical recycling.
recycled-nylon.structure: Recycled nylon has the same repeating amide (-CO-NH-) backbone as virgin polyamide, with hydrogen bonds between chains forming crystalline regions that give strength and a high melting point. Nylon 6 rebuilt from purified caprolactam can be chemically indistinguishable from virgin nylon 6. Mechanically recycled nylon, remelted without depolymerization, can undergo chain scission and lower molecular weight and may carry pigments, additives and contaminants from its source, which limits use in fine filament yarns. Fiber morphology is set by the spinneret, drawing and texturing, not by the waste source.
recycled-nylon.process: Mechanical recycling cleans, shreds and remelts clean, single-polymer waste, typically pre-consumer, into pellets for extrusion. Chemical recycling of nylon 6 exploits its ability to revert to monomer. Routes studied include acidic, hydrothermal, alcoholysis and alkaline depolymerization; laboratory work has reported about 92.5 percent caprolactam yield in subcritical water at about 300 C and 10 MPa, and about 94 percent over a ruthenium on zirconia catalyst at 350 C under hydrogen. Recovered caprolactam is purified, repolymerized, melt spun, drawn and textured like virgin polymer. Enzymatic routes remain early: the best enzyme in one screen hydrolyzed only about 0.67 percent of a nylon 6 film.
recycled-nylon.performance: Performance tracks polymer type and processing, not waste origin. Chemically recycled nylon 6 is intended to match virgin grades in tenacity, elongation, abrasion resistance and elastic recovery, which is why it can be used in hosiery and swimwear. Like virgin nylon it absorbs less moisture than natural fibers but more than polyester, dyes with acid dyes through its amine end groups, melts and drips in flame, and yellows and loses strength under prolonged UV. Mechanically recycled grades can show more variable dye uptake because molecular weight and end-group content vary.
recycled-nylon.identify: Burn testing (indicative only; nylon melts, drips and gives a distinctive odor, so test with care) and FTIR identify polyamide, and melting behavior measured by DSC can help separate nylon 6 from nylon 6,6. None of these methods can show whether the polymer is recycled, because chemically recycled nylon is the same molecule as virgin nylon. Recycled claims therefore depend on chain-of-custody certification and on how the producer accounts for recycled input, which buyers should ask to see.
recycled-nylon.labeling: The generic name remains nylon in the US, and Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 uses polyamide or nylon. A recycled claim is an environmental marketing claim; in the US the FTC's Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260) require substantiation and limit pre-consumer recycled claims to material diverted from the waste stream rather than scrap routinely reused in the same process. Textile Exchange's Recycled Claim Standard and Global Recycled Standard certify recycled input through the supply chain. Program names such as Aquafil's ECONYL are trademarks, not generic fiber names, and labels still need the generic name.
recycled-nylon.past: Nylon 6,6 emerged from Wallace Carothers's polymer research at DuPont in the 1930s, and nylon 6 followed from caprolactam chemistry in Germany; both became major apparel and carpet polymers. Recycling began with reuse of production waste, while the chemical reversibility of nylon 6 later enabled depolymerization to monomer. Current research seeks cleaner routes: a 2026 life cycle assessment of four real-world nylon 6 remonomerization processes found the solvent-free alkaline (NaOH) route cut global warming potential by about 80 percent relative to fossil caprolactam, to about 1.46 kg CO2-eq per kg, while no route met a 1.5 C carbon budget.
